## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

\begin{marginfigure}
\mlagentstack{0}{0}{0}{0}{100}{0}
\end{marginfigure}

*Attention state has a cost even when the agent is not generating.*

An agent's context becomes physical state when the serving system computes the keys and values used by attention. Retaining that state can spare later computation, but it occupies memory that other calls could use. Long contexts enlarge the claim; branches may duplicate it; tool waits can extend its lifetime without producing another token. The serving system must allocate this state as it grows, share compatible prefixes, and decide when to keep, move, or reconstruct paused state. The harness shapes these choices through the context it sends and the work it launches, even when a hosted service owns the allocation policy. In H·S·A terms, this chapter follows the physical cost of State as Horizon grows, and establishes how that cost constrains the work a serving system can support.

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}

\newpage

:::

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Estimate retained attention-state memory from model geometry, token count, and storage precision
- Explain how block allocation and prefix sharing reduce unused and duplicated memory
- Distinguish compatible, available prefix reuse from the applicability of the underlying information
- Evaluate scheduling and paused-state policies against memory pressure and resume latency
- Interpret memory-fit bounds alongside workload, latency, and throughput measurements

:::

## The Footprint of Retained Attention State {#sec-vol3-kvcache-geometry}

The connection-pool repair has reached a candidate revision, r18. Its targeted reproducer passes, but that result does not yet establish that the broader interface behaves correctly. Consider a new illustrative serving situation: the harness submits a fully serialized request of 32,768 tokens and then launches an integration test that takes 45 seconds. Suppose the service retains the compatible attention state on the accelerator throughout that wait. The model generates nothing during the test, yet the retained state occupies memory that another request could use. Neither the end of a model turn nor a tool wait inherently requires this retention; keeping the state is the service policy being examined.

@Sec-vol3-context-engineering established how the harness selects and refreshes the information in a call. The present question is what it costs to store and reuse the computation derived from those tokens. The application caller controls its submitted context and any cache controls the service exposes. The serving operator controls the allocator, placement, and retention policy. These may belong to the same organization, but an application using a hosted model cannot assume that it can pin or evict particular accelerator buffers.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/hsa_locator_s.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="H·S·A locator with the State axis highlighted."}

*State becomes a physical resource claim inside the serving system.*
:::

The key-value (KV) cache stores intermediate vectors computed by the model, not another copy of the prompt text. For causal attention, a new token attends to earlier tokens through their keys and values. Keeping those vectors avoids computing them again when decoding subsequent tokens. The cache is therefore derived state: reconstructing it requires the original token sequence and compatible model computation, not merely a summary with similar meaning.

For a decoder with full causal attention and uniform layer geometry, each retained token contributes a key vector and a value vector at every layer. Let $N_L$ be the number of layers, $H_{\text{KV}}$ the number of key-value heads per layer, $d_{\text{head}}$ the dimension of each head, and $s_{\text{elem}}$ the bytes stored per element. Counting the two vectors gives

$$m_{\text{token}} = 2 \cdot N_L \cdot H_{\text{KV}} \cdot d_{\text{head}} \cdot s_{\text{elem}}$$ {#eq-mem-token}

bytes per retained token. A sequence with KV state for $S$ tokens consequently has payload $M_{\text{KV}} = S \cdot m_{\text{token}}$. Here $S$ counts tokens whose keys and values have actually been computed, including generated tokens that have been processed by the model. Returning a newly sampled token does not by itself guarantee that the service has already computed that token's KV state for reuse.

The head count in @eq-mem-token is the number of stored key-value heads, not necessarily the number of query heads. Grouped-query attention lets several query heads use the same key-value head, reducing the stored head count relative to an otherwise comparable multi-head design [@ainslie2023gqa]. This is a property of the model architecture. It is not permission for an allocator to discard distinct heads from an existing model without changing its computation.

The formula counts tensor payload only. Allocation granularity, alignment, block metadata, and any precision-specific scales add storage beyond that payload. It also assumes full attention over the retained sequence. Architectures with local attention or compressed latent state require their own accounting. These distinctions matter before any capacity number is interpreted as a deployment limit.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: kv-geometry-calc
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ RETAINED ATTENTION STATE: PAYLOAD AND IDEALIZED RESIDENT FIT
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-vol3-kvcache-geometry; nbk-05-sizing-the-attention-state-for.
# │ Goal: Derive a token's KV payload and a node's unshared memory-fit bound.
# │ Show: 327,680 bytes/token; 526.0 GB pool; 195/48/12 resident sequences.
# │ How: Registry geometry and capacity, FP16 storage, local runtime reserve.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_int, fmt_memory, fmt_params, fmt_math

class KvGeometry:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ─────────────────────────────────
    _model = Models.Language.Llama3_70B
    _node = Systems.Nodes.DGX_H100
    n_layers = _model.layers
    n_kv_heads = _model.kv_heads
    d_head = _model.hidden_dim // _model.heads
    element_size = BYTES_FP16
    n_acc = _node.accelerators_per_node
    runtime_reserve = 20 * GB  # scenario: activations and runtime buffers
    ctx_short, ctx_agent, ctx_long = 8_192, 32_768, 131_072  # scenario token counts

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ──────────────────────────────
    bytes_per_token = calc_kv_cache_size(n_layers, n_kv_heads, d_head, 1, 1, element_size)
    kv_short = bytes_per_token * ctx_short
    kv_agent = bytes_per_token * ctx_agent
    kv_long = bytes_per_token * ctx_long
    node_hbm = n_acc * _node.accelerator.memory.capacity
    weights = _model.size_in_bytes(BYTES_FP16)
    kv_pool = node_hbm - weights - runtime_reserve
    conc_short = int((kv_pool / kv_short).to("").magnitude)
    conc_agent = int((kv_pool / kv_agent).to("").magnitude)
    conc_long = int((kv_pool / kv_long).to("").magnitude)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD ────────────────────────────────
    check(bytes_per_token.to(byte).magnitude == 327_680, "Registry KV geometry changed")
    check(525.9 < kv_pool.to(GB).magnitude < 526.1, "Expected canonical decimal-GB pool")
    check((conc_short, conc_agent, conc_long) == (195, 48, 12), "Resident-fit bounds changed")
    check(conc_agent * kv_agent <= kv_pool < (conc_agent + 1) * kv_agent, "Floor bound must bracket pool")
    check(kv_long / kv_short == ctx_long / ctx_short, "Payload must scale linearly with retained tokens")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ───────────────────────────────
    params_str = fmt_params(_model.parameters, scale="B", precision=1)
    n_acc_str = fmt_int(n_acc)
    ctx_short_str = fmt_int(ctx_short)
    ctx_agent_str = fmt_int(ctx_agent)
    ctx_long_str = fmt_int(ctx_long)
    kv_short_str = fmt_memory(kv_short, unit=GB, precision=1)
    kv_agent_str = fmt_memory(kv_agent, unit=GB, precision=1)
    kv_long_str = fmt_memory(kv_long, unit=GB, precision=1)
    node_hbm_str = fmt_memory(node_hbm, unit=GB, precision=1)
    weights_str = fmt_memory(weights, unit=GB, precision=1)
    reserve_str = fmt_memory(runtime_reserve, unit=GB, precision=0)
    kv_pool_str = fmt_memory(kv_pool, unit=GB, precision=1)
    conc_short_str = fmt_int(conc_short)
    conc_agent_str = fmt_int(conc_agent)
    conc_long_str = fmt_int(conc_long)
    token_math = fmt_math(
        rf"m_{{\text{{token}}}} = 2 \times {n_layers} \times {n_kv_heads} \times {d_head} \times {element_size.to(byte).magnitude:g} = {bytes_per_token.to(byte).magnitude:,.0f}\;\text{{bytes/token}}"
    )
    trajectory_math = fmt_math(
        rf"M_{{\text{{KV}}}} = {ctx_agent:,} \times {bytes_per_token.to(byte).magnitude:,.0f}\;\text{{bytes}} \approx {kv_agent.to(GB).magnitude:.1f}\;\text{{GB}}"
    )
    pool_math = fmt_math(
        rf"{node_hbm.to(GB).magnitude:.1f} - {weights.to(GB).magnitude:.1f} - {runtime_reserve.to(GB).magnitude:g} \approx {kv_pool.to(GB).magnitude:.1f}\;\text{{GB}}"
    )
    fit_math = fmt_math(rf"\left\lfloor {kv_pool.to(GB).magnitude:.9f} / {kv_agent.to(GB).magnitude:.9f} \right\rfloor = {conc_agent}")
```

The worked estimate uses the Llama 3 70B model geometry, with `{python} KvGeometry.params_str` parameters, and a DGX H100 node containing `{python} KvGeometry.n_acc_str` accelerators. This is a different deployment assumption from the single-device, 8-bit weight-read illustration in @sec-vol3-foundation-model-cost. Here both weights and KV use 16-bit storage, and the weights are sharded across the node. Aggregate capacity arithmetic assumes that the shards and their KV state can be balanced across devices without additional replicated copies. A real deployment must also satisfy each device's limit. @Fig-vol3-context-window-anatomy traces one agent context of this length from its logical zones through that geometry to the number of such contexts the node can hold.

::: {#fig-vol3-context-window-anatomy fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**From Agent Context to KV State**: A 32,768-token agent context, divided into system prompt, tool schemas, workspace, turn history, and the latest observation, becomes key and value tensors at every layer. The grouped-query model's per-token footprint then sets how many such contexts fit in the node's KV pool, before allocator overhead and headroom." fig-alt="Top panel divides a 32,768-token context into five labeled zones with token counts, grouped as a shared prefix, growing history, and active turn. Arrows lead to a bottom panel listing model dimensions, the per-token and per-context KV footprint, and resident counts of 195 and 48 at 8,192 and 32,768 tokens on an eight-accelerator node."}
![](images/svg/prompt_context_window_anatomy.svg)
:::

::: {#nbk-05-sizing-the-attention-state-for .callout-notebook title="Sizing the attention state of an agent trajectory"}

**Problem**: The node provides `{python} KvGeometry.node_hbm_str` of aggregate accelerator memory. Its weights occupy `{python} KvGeometry.weights_str`, and this scenario reserves `{python} KvGeometry.reserve_str` for activations and runtime buffers. How many independent, unshared sequences fit in the remaining memory at each of the three context lengths below?

**Math**: The key and value count gives `{python} KvGeometry.token_math`. At the illustrative request length, `{python} KvGeometry.trajectory_math`.

The memory available for KV payload is `{python} KvGeometry.pool_math`. Dividing that pool by a sequence's payload and rounding down gives the resident-fit bound. Using unrounded quantities for the division, the illustrative request gives `{python} KvGeometry.fit_math`. @Tbl-vol3-kv-payload-fit applies the same calculation at three retained lengths.

|         **Retained tokens**         |    **KV payload per sequence**     |        **Sequences that fit**        |
|:-----------------------------------:|:----------------------------------:|:------------------------------------:|
| `{python} KvGeometry.ctx_short_str` | `{python} KvGeometry.kv_short_str` | `{python} KvGeometry.conc_short_str` |
| `{python} KvGeometry.ctx_agent_str` | `{python} KvGeometry.kv_agent_str` | `{python} KvGeometry.conc_agent_str` |
|  `{python} KvGeometry.ctx_long_str` | `{python} KvGeometry.kv_long_str`  | `{python} KvGeometry.conc_long_str`  |

: **Payload and resident fit**: Each sequence stores its own full-attention state; the calculation excludes allocator overhead and additional headroom. {#tbl-vol3-kv-payload-fit tbl-colwidths="[28,38,34]"}

**Systems insight**: The same `{python} KvGeometry.kv_pool_str` pool holds fewer sequences as retained context grows. These counts describe payload residency before allocator overhead or safety headroom. They do not establish how many requests can meet a latency target or how many turns the node can complete per second.

:::

The estimate separates two costs that can otherwise be confused. The model's weight storage is shared by the requests it serves; each independent sequence adds its own attention state. A single sequence need not be larger than the weights for KV capacity to matter. Across many sequences, long contexts can consume the remaining memory even when the model itself fits comfortably. Shared prefixes can reduce that total, but only when the serving system retains and safely reuses compatible state. The harness also moves each trajectory along the rows of @tbl-vol3-kv-payload-fit: keeping every call's context near its selected working set (principle \ref{pri-vol3-attention-working-set}) holds a trajectory near the shorter rows, while a harness that accumulates every observation drives it toward the last.

Architecture and precision change the payload before allocation begins. A model designed to retain fewer key-value heads or latent vectors can use less state, but it is not a lossless storage transformation of an arbitrary full-attention model. Lower-precision KV storage can also reduce payload, with additional scale or format overhead and possible changes to model outputs. Its value depends on supported kernels and validation on the intended tasks. Neither choice eliminates the need to manage the lifetime and ownership of the state that remains.

For the repair agent, retaining state during the integration test is one such lifetime decision. The caller may prefer a faster resume, while the operator must weigh that benefit against competing requests. Before comparing those policies, the allocator must turn the payload estimate into actual storage. Reserving every sequence's largest possible future size can waste the pool well before its useful tensor contents reach capacity.

## Memory Fragmentation {#sec-vol3-kvcache-fragmentation}

The repair agent's next request can grow when the integration test returns a log. The serving operator must provide space for that additional KV state without knowing the final length of every concurrent request. The footprint calculation gives the bytes needed for tokens already processed. An allocation policy determines how much additional memory is reserved, whether a growing request must move, and when released capacity can serve another request.

### Reservation and growth

One policy reserves a contiguous tensor buffer for the configured token cap at admission. Within that cap, the request can add KV entries without enlarging its allocation. This reserves its KV capacity, not every resource needed to finish the call: temporary activations, runtime buffers, and other allocations can still exhaust device memory. The unused portion of the reservation also cannot serve another request while the reservation remains committed.

```{python}
#| label: kv-static-reservation-calc
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ STATIC RESERVATION
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-vol3-kvcache-fragmentation reservation example.
# │ Goal: Separate final-length utilization from a resident-fit bound.
# │ Show: Final-length efficiency of 6.25 percent; 48 full-cap reservations.
# │ How: Registry model and node, local cap/mean and runtime reserve assumptions.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_int, fmt_memory, fmt_percent
from mlsysim.physics.agents import calc_kv_cache_bytes_per_token

class StaticReservation:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
    model = Models.Language.Llama3_70B
    node = Systems.Nodes.DGX_H100
    elem_size = BYTES_FP16
    runtime_reserve = 20 * GB  # scenario: node-wide activations/runtime reserve
    s_max = 32_768  # illustrative deployment cap, not a model specification
    mean_final_tokens = 2_048  # hypothetical mean FINAL length, not a trace mean

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    bytes_per_token = calc_kv_cache_bytes_per_token(model, bytes_per_elem=elem_size)
    node_hbm = node.accelerators_per_node * node.accelerator.memory.capacity
    weights = model.size_in_bytes(elem_size)
    pool = node_hbm - weights - runtime_reserve
    reservation = s_max * bytes_per_token
    reservations = int((pool / reservation).to("").magnitude)
    efficiency = mean_final_tokens / s_max

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(pool.to(byte).magnitude > 0, "The KV pool must be positive")
    check(reservations * reservation <= pool < (reservations + 1) * reservation, "The count must be the whole-reservation fit bound")
    check(0 < mean_final_tokens <= s_max, "Final lengths must respect the cap")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────────
    s_max_str = fmt_int(s_max)
    mean_final_tokens_str = fmt_int(mean_final_tokens)
    pool_gb_str = fmt_memory(pool, unit=GB, precision=1)
    reservation_gb_str = fmt_memory(reservation, unit=GB, precision=2)
    reservations_str = fmt_int(reservations)
    efficiency_str = fmt_percent(efficiency, precision=2, style="prose")
```

For the Llama-3-70B model on the eight-accelerator node, retaining the same 16-bit weight and KV representation and node-wide runtime reserve leaves a KV pool of `{python} StaticReservation.pool_gb_str`. A cap of `{python} StaticReservation.s_max_str` tokens requires `{python} StaticReservation.reservation_gb_str` per reservation. Dividing the pool by that reservation and rounding down gives `{python} StaticReservation.reservations_str` resident reservations, assuming balanced sharding and no additional overhead outside the stated reserve. This is a memory-fit calculation, not a throughput prediction.

Suppose a different, hypothetical request population finishes at a mean length of `{python} StaticReservation.mean_final_tokens_str` tokens. Its mean final-length utilization is `{python} StaticReservation.mean_final_tokens_str` divided by `{python} StaticReservation.s_max_str`, or `{python} StaticReservation.efficiency_str`. This comparison describes how much of each reservation is populated at completion. It does not measure utilization over time: long-lived requests and paused trajectories contribute more memory occupancy than short-lived requests, and an expanding request has not yet reached its final length. Measured systems confirm the pattern. In the serving systems profiled when paged KV allocation was introduced, only 20.4 to 38.2 percent of KV memory held actual token state, with the rest lost to reservation slack and fragmentation [@kwon2023vllm].

A second policy grows a contiguous allocation as tokens arrive. If adjacent capacity is unavailable, an allocate-copy-release implementation obtains a larger buffer, copies the initialized KV entries, and then releases the old buffer. During that copy, both allocations consume space. Other implementations can use different allocation or remapping mechanisms; a synchronous allocation stall is not an inevitable property of every growing tensor. Here, contiguous means a contiguous range in the allocator's address space, not necessarily adjacent physical DRAM cells. Accelerators already support virtual memory. The relevant restriction is whether this serving allocator and attention kernel require the sequence's KV tensor to occupy one such range.

### Two kinds of unused capacity

Unused reserved slots and disconnected free extents create different problems. The distinction in @tbl-vol3-kv-fragmentation-taxonomies determines whether releasing slack or changing the allocation granularity can help.

| **Condition**          | **Where capacity is unavailable**                           | **Consequence**                                                               |
|:-----------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Internal fragmentation | Inside an allocation, beyond its initialized entries        | Other requests cannot use the reserved slots                                  |
| External fragmentation | In separate free extents of a variable-size allocation pool | A contiguous request can fail even when aggregate free capacity is sufficient |

: **Unused KV capacity**: Reservation slack belongs to an allocation; external fragmentation concerns free space that cannot satisfy a particular contiguous request. {#tbl-vol3-kv-fragmentation-taxonomies tbl-colwidths="[22,40,38]"}

For a concrete external-fragmentation example, suppose an allocator has three free extents of exactly 256 token slots each, separated by live allocations. A request requiring 512 contiguous slots cannot fit in any extent, although the free extents together have sufficient capacity. This conclusion depends on the stated contiguous-allocation requirement. It does not claim that the underlying accelerator lacks address translation or that every serving allocator has the same limitation.

In the repair workload, a tool wait matters only if the service retains the allocation. Under the chapter's initial retention policy, the paused trajectory continues to occupy KV space while another request may need to grow. An operator therefore needs both a space-efficient allocation unit and an explicit lifetime policy. Fixed-size blocks address the allocation problem first; they do not by themselves decide how long a completed or paused request should retain state.

## Paged KV Allocation {#sec-vol3-kvcache-pagedattention}

When the integration-test log extends the repair context, the serving engine need not relocate the entire existing KV tensor. It can allocate additional fixed-size blocks and add their identifiers to the request's block table. The attention kernel follows that table when reading earlier token positions. PagedAttention demonstrated this combination of block allocation and attention over noncontiguous KV storage [@kwon2023vllm]. Its lineage is paged virtual memory, which the Atlas one-level store introduced to decouple a program's contiguous address space from scattered physical frames [@kilburn1962onelevel]. The block table applies the same indirection to token positions, so a sequence can grow without a contiguous extent.

::: {#dfn-paged-kv-cache .callout-definition title="Paged attention KV-cache block table"}

***Paged attention KV-cache block table***\index{Paged attention!block table definition}\index{KV cache!block table definition} is a per-sequence software mapping from logical token blocks to the physical KV blocks that store their initialized key and value entries.

1. **Significance**: A sequence can grow by acquiring another block without relocating its existing blocks.
2. **Distinction**: The table maps token positions for the attention kernel; it is not the accelerator's hardware page table.
3. **Common pitfall**: A mapped block has allocated capacity, but only its initialized token entries may be read as valid KV state.

:::

### Mapping tokens to blocks

Consider an illustrative block size of four tokens, chosen to make the mapping visible rather than to recommend a production setting. A ten-token prefix occupies logical blocks 0, 1, and 2. Its block table is `[3, 7, 9]`: positions 0–3 reside in physical block 3, positions 4–7 in block 7, and positions 8–9 in the first two slots of block 9. Physical IDs are labels in the allocator's pool, not token positions or memory addresses.

For any token position, the kernel identifies its logical block by integer division by the block size, uses the table to find the physical block, and selects the token's offset by taking the remainder. Thus position 9 selects logical block 2, physical block 9, and slot 1. The actual address also depends on the layer, KV head, and tensor layout. This software lookup preserves logical sequence order even when physical block IDs are scattered. @Fig-vol3-pagedattention-mapping traces the ten-token example through the table into the pool, and previews the copy-on-write step that prefix sharing requires.

::: {#fig-vol3-pagedattention-mapping fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Block Table Indirection and Tail Copy-on-Write**: Panel (a) follows each logical block through its table entry to a physical block scattered among other requests' blocks; position 9 resolves to logical block 2, then to physical block 9, slot 1. Panel (b) shows two candidates that share the full blocks 3 and 7, while candidate B's private append first copies the two initialized entries of the shared tail into block 14." fig-alt="Panel a shows three logical blocks of four slots holding positions 0 to 9, arrows to a block table with entries 3, 7, and 9, and elbow arrows to physical blocks 3, 7, and 9 in a row of twelve blocks, some used by other requests. A card shows the lookup for position 9. Panel b shows candidate A's table 3, 7, 9 and candidate B's table 3, 7, 14, shared blocks 3 and 7 with two owners, and an arrow copying slots from block 9 into block 14, where position 10 is written."}
![](images/svg/paged_attention_virtual_memory.svg)
:::

Within a pool of interchangeable fixed-size blocks, a new block request can use any free block. Variable-sized free holes no longer prevent that allocation. This removes external fragmentation at this pool's block granularity, not every possible source of device-memory waste. Metadata, temporary buffers, different allocation pools, and unused final-block slots still consume capacity.

### Block size and tail waste

The last block may contain unused slots. If a block holds $p$ tokens, the local tail-waste bound is $0 \leq \Delta_{\text{tail}} \leq p-1$, where $\Delta_{\text{tail}}$ counts uninitialized slots in the final allocated block. The mean is $(p-1)/2$ only if sequence lengths have uniformly distributed remainders modulo $p$. It is not a universal property of request lengths. In particular, a length divisible by the block size has no tail waste.

Smaller blocks reduce this tail bound and allow finer-grained sharing and copying. They also require more table entries for the same context and more block-management work. Larger blocks reverse those tendencies and may suit a kernel's access pattern better. The appropriate size depends on the length distribution, branching behavior, and implementation, not a universal waste percentage or bandwidth guarantee.

```{python}
#| label: lego-05-physical-block-sizing
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ PHYSICAL BLOCK SIZING
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: notebook nbk-05-sizing-physical-blocks-for-a.
# │ Goal: Convert allocation granularity into physical storage and a tail bound.
# │ Show: Node-wide block footprints and maximum tail slack for 16/64 tokens.
# │ How: Registry model geometry and precision; explicitly hypothetical sizes.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_int, fmt_memory
from mlsysim.physics.agents import calc_kv_cache_bytes_per_token

class PhysicalBlockSizing:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
    model = Models.Language.Llama3_70B
    elem_size = BYTES_FP16
    small_tokens, large_tokens = 16, 64  # illustrative allocator choices

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    bytes_per_token = calc_kv_cache_bytes_per_token(model, bytes_per_elem=elem_size)
    small_block = small_tokens * bytes_per_token
    large_block = large_tokens * bytes_per_token
    small_tail_tokens = small_tokens - 1
    large_tail_tokens = large_tokens - 1
    small_tail = small_tail_tokens * bytes_per_token
    large_tail = large_tail_tokens * bytes_per_token

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(0 * byte <= small_tail < small_block, "Tail must fit inside one block")
    check(0 * byte <= large_tail < large_block, "Tail must fit inside one block")
    check(small_block * large_tokens == large_block * small_tokens, "Both block sizes must use the same KV geometry")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────────
    bytes_per_token_str = fmt_memory(bytes_per_token, unit=byte, precision=0)
    small_tokens_str = fmt_int(small_tokens)
    large_tokens_str = fmt_int(large_tokens)
    small_block_mb_str = fmt_memory(small_block, unit=MB, precision=2)
    large_block_mb_str = fmt_memory(large_block, unit=MB, precision=2)
    small_tail_tokens_str = fmt_int(small_tail_tokens)
    large_tail_tokens_str = fmt_int(large_tail_tokens)
    small_tail_mb_str = fmt_memory(small_tail, unit=MB, precision=2)
    large_tail_mb_str = fmt_memory(large_tail, unit=MB, precision=2)
```

::: {#nbk-05-sizing-physical-blocks-for-a .callout-notebook title="Converting block size into KV storage"}

**Problem**: With the same Llama-3-70B geometry and 16-bit KV representation, what storage granularity and maximum tail slack follow from two different block sizes?

**Math**: Each token requires `{python} PhysicalBlockSizing.bytes_per_token_str` across all model layers and heads. Multiplying that footprint by `{python} PhysicalBlockSizing.small_tokens_str` tokens gives `{python} PhysicalBlockSizing.small_block_mb_str` per block. Multiplying by `{python} PhysicalBlockSizing.large_tokens_str` instead gives `{python} PhysicalBlockSizing.large_block_mb_str`. These are aggregate footprints across the model's shards, not the allocation on each accelerator.

The maximum unused tail has one fewer slot than a full block. The smaller block can therefore leave `{python} PhysicalBlockSizing.small_tail_tokens_str` slots, or `{python} PhysicalBlockSizing.small_tail_mb_str`, unused; the larger can leave `{python} PhysicalBlockSizing.large_tail_tokens_str` slots, or `{python} PhysicalBlockSizing.large_tail_mb_str`, unused.

**Systems insight**: Allocation granularity determines the maximum slack at each unshared tail. These bounds do not predict average waste without a workload distribution, and they exclude block tables and other runtime storage.

:::

```{python}
#| label: kv-paged-waste-calc
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ PAGED ALLOCATION PAYOFF
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-vol3-kvcache-pagedattention, paragraph after
# │          nbk-05-sizing-physical-blocks-for-a.
# │ Goal: Answer the static-reservation count with what paging admits under a
# │       stated length distribution.
# │ Show: 0.4 percent tail waste at 16-token blocks, 1.5 percent at 64;
# │       780 paged sequences vs. 48 full-cap reservations (about 16x).
# │ How: calc_expected_paged_kv_tokens over a capped-exponential length model
# │      (modeling assumption) with StaticReservation's mean, cap, and pool.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.physics.memory import calc_expected_paged_kv_tokens
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_int, fmt_percent, fmt_multiple

class PagedWaste:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
    block_small = PhysicalBlockSizing.small_tokens
    block_large = PhysicalBlockSizing.large_tokens
    mean_tokens = StaticReservation.mean_final_tokens  # same hypothetical mean final length
    s_max = StaticReservation.s_max
    bytes_per_token = StaticReservation.bytes_per_token
    pool = StaticReservation.pool

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    alloc_small, frag_small = calc_expected_paged_kv_tokens(mean_tokens, s_max, block_small)
    alloc_large, frag_large = calc_expected_paged_kv_tokens(mean_tokens, s_max, block_large)
    fit_paged = int((pool / (alloc_small * bytes_per_token)).to("").magnitude)
    gain = fit_paged / StaticReservation.reservations

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(0 < frag_small < frag_large < 0.02, "Larger blocks must waste more, and both only a few percent")
    check(mean_tokens <= alloc_small < mean_tokens + block_small, "Expected allocation exceeds the mean by less than one block")
    check(fit_paged == 780, "Paged fit on the canonical pool changed")
    check(15 < gain < 17, "Prose claims about sixteen times as many sequences")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────────
    frag_small_str = fmt_percent(frag_small, precision=1, style="prose")
    frag_large_str = fmt_percent(frag_large, precision=1, style="prose")
    fit_paged_str = fmt_int(fit_paged)
    gain_mult_str = fmt_multiple(round(gain))  # prose says "roughly"
```

The tail bounds become an expected waste once a length distribution is stated. Model final lengths as exponential with the hypothetical mean of `{python} StaticReservation.mean_final_tokens_str` tokens, capped at the `{python} StaticReservation.s_max_str`-token limit used for static reservation. Under that assumption, `{python} PhysicalBlockSizing.small_tokens_str`-token blocks leave `{python} PagedWaste.frag_small_str` of allocated KV memory unused and `{python} PhysicalBlockSizing.large_tokens_str`-token blocks leave `{python} PagedWaste.frag_large_str`. Dividing the pool that admitted `{python} StaticReservation.reservations_str` full-cap reservations by the expected paged allocation gives about `{python} PagedWaste.fit_paged_str` sequences, roughly `{python} PagedWaste.gain_mult_str` as many. That is the payoff of paging. Allocation tracks the tokens a sequence has actually produced rather than the cap it might reach. The count is a mean memory-fit estimate under a modeling assumption; the resident count fluctuates with the lengths actually present, and memory fit says nothing about throughput.

### Sharing a prefix without sharing its future writes

```{python}
#| label: kv-fork-copy-calc
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ FORK COST UNDER CONTIGUOUS ALLOCATION
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-vol3-kvcache-pagedattention, prefix-sharing paragraph.
# │ Goal: Size the tensor copy that block sharing avoids when candidates fork.
# │ Show: 10.7 GB copied for four candidates of an 8,192-token prefix.
# │ How: Registry KV geometry (PhysicalBlockSizing); scenario prefix and fan-out.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_int, fmt_memory

class ForkCopy:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
    prefix_tokens = 8_192  # scenario: processed prefix shared by the candidates
    branches = 4  # scenario: sampled candidate repairs
    bytes_per_token = PhysicalBlockSizing.bytes_per_token

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    copied = branches * prefix_tokens * bytes_per_token

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(branches == 4, "Prose spells out four candidates")
    check(10 < copied.to(GB).magnitude < 11, "Prose describes roughly ten gigabytes copied")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────────
    prefix_str = fmt_int(prefix_tokens)
    copied_str = fmt_memory(copied, unit=GB, precision=1)
```

Deliberation that samples several candidates to buy evidence (principle \ref{pri-vol3-test-time-scaling}) makes forks routine. Candidate repairs can begin from the same processed prefix and then generate different continuations. Their block tables may refer to the same immutable prefix blocks if the model computation is compatible and the service permits sharing. No full-prefix tensor copy is needed when the candidates are created. The saving is large at agent context lengths. A contiguous allocator that deep-copies an `{python} ForkCopy.prefix_str`-token prefix into four candidates writes `{python} ForkCopy.copied_str` of KV state for the Llama-3-70B geometry, while block-table duplication copies none of that payload. The runtime still constructs or shares metadata and records ownership; copying a block table and updating its references can require work proportional to its number of entries.

The partial tail needs special treatment. Two candidates cannot independently append into the same shared writable slot. In the ten-token example, both candidates initially refer to `[3, 7, 9]`. Before candidate B writes position 10, the runtime allocates block 14, copies the two initialized entries from block 9, and redirects B's last table entry. The write then occurs at slot 2 of block 14. This copy-on-write operation leaves candidate A's state unchanged. @Tbl-vol3-kv-cow-trace follows the ownership change; its counts assume these two candidates are the only owners.

| **State**                     | **Candidate A table** | **Candidate B table** | **Physical ownership**                                   |
|:------------------------------|:----------------------|:----------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------|
| Before append                 | `[3, 7, 9]`           | `[3, 7, 9]`           | Blocks 3, 7, and 9 each have two owners                  |
| After B's private-tail append | `[3, 7, 9]`           | `[3, 7, 14]`          | Blocks 3 and 7 retain two owners; 9 and 14 each have one |

: **Partial-tail copy-on-write**: Full prefix blocks remain shared while the initialized portion of the tail is copied before a private append. The block IDs label allocations; they do not imply contiguous addresses. {#tbl-vol3-kv-cow-trace tbl-colwidths="[23,20,20,37]"}

This is different from appending at a full-block boundary. After a twelve-token prefix in four-token blocks, position 12 starts a new logical block. The appending candidate acquires a fresh block; it does not copy an old tail. A private partial tail can likewise accept another entry without a copy. The necessary operation depends on both the fill level and ownership of the block being modified.

When a candidate is discarded, its references are released. A block returns to the free pool only after all ownership that requires its contents has ended and any in-flight readers or writers have completed. A dormant prefix-cache entry can still own a block after active requests release it; conversely, the service may make such cached blocks reclaimable under its eviction policy. Reference bookkeeping and completion fences must therefore prevent reuse while an operation still accesses the old contents. Logical bytes summed across candidates are not the physical storage total when blocks are shared.

::: {#chk-05-memory-fragmentation .callout-checkpoint title="Reasoning about KV allocation"}

The allocation policy must preserve each sequence's state while managing capacity shared by many requests.

- [ ] **Reservation efficiency**: Can you explain why a mean final length does not determine memory occupancy over time or guarantee a safe admission count?
- [ ] **External fragmentation**: Can you identify why the three free extents in the example cannot satisfy its contiguous request, and why a fixed-size block pool changes that condition?
- [ ] **Tail ownership**: Can you trace a private append to a shared partial tail and distinguish it from an append at a full-block boundary?
- [ ] **Reclamation**: Can you explain why ending an active request does not always make its blocks immediately reusable?

:::

Block allocation separates logical sequence growth from the placement of its KV state. Sharing then allows compatible candidates to use one physical copy of their common history. Reuse across later model calls needs an additional mechanism: the service must find compatible state that remains available and decide whether retaining it is worthwhile. That is the role of prefix caching.

## Prefix Caching Across Turns {#sec-vol3-kvcache-radix-tree}

Block sharing lets related trajectories reuse attention state without copying their entire history. A later request can benefit even when it was not created by an explicit fork. In the connection-pool repair, the call that reads the integration-test result may begin with the same instructions, tool definitions, and earlier observations as the preceding call. If the service retained the corresponding KV state, it can attach that state to the new request and prefill the remaining input. Prefix caching makes this reuse possible across request boundaries; it does not guarantee that completed requests remain resident.

### Compatibility before reuse

For the causal full-attention model used here, reusable state corresponds to an exact input prefix, not a passage with similar meaning. Matching token IDs is necessary but is not the whole compatibility check. The state must also belong to compatible model weights, adapters, positions, attention masks, and other computation settings. Where an input contains images or other nontext data, matching placeholder tokens is insufficient; the underlying model inputs must match as well. A serving system must identify these dependencies in its cache key or otherwise enforce them before reuse.

Compatibility, availability, and permission answer different questions. Compatible tensors may have been evicted or may require a transfer before they can be used. Available tensors may belong to a different isolation domain and therefore be ineligible for sharing. The prefix a request can reuse is limited by all three conditions, not just by the longest string found in an index. Generated tokens qualify only after their corresponding KV state has actually been computed and retained.

These conditions are also separate from whether an observation remains appropriate for the task. Changing the repository from r17 to r18 does not alter tensors already computed for an unchanged prompt describing r17. Those tensors may remain numerically compatible with that old prompt even though the prompt no longer supplies the evidence needed to judge r18. The selection policy in @sec-vol3-context-engineering determines which evidence to include. Once the caller refreshes or replaces that evidence in the serialized input, prefix matching stops at the first changed token. A cache hit is not a freshness check.

### Finding usable prefix state

A *radix prefix cache* indexes token sequences with a compressed prefix tree, whose edges may represent several tokens rather than one. Following matching edges from the root identifies a common prefix and the associated KV storage [@zheng2024sglang]. The service must then obtain usable ownership of that storage before eviction can reclaim it. Lookup is not constant time: it involves examining the request prefix and consulting the index. A radix tree is one implementation, not a requirement for correct caching. An index of blocks keyed by their contents and preceding prefix can support the same reuse contract.

The match must extend from the beginning of the input. A repeated passage after a changed earlier token is not, in general, reusable as an independent suffix: its attention state was computed under a different preceding context. This is the physical consequence of the stable-prefix layout in @sec-vol3-context-engineering-staging. Keeping volatile fields later preserves more opportunities for reuse, while rewriting an earlier region shortens the common prefix. Compaction need not destroy an unchanged prefix before the rewritten region.

Block boundaries create a policy choice, not a different definition of compatibility. Return to the illustrative ten-token prefix in four-token blocks `[3, 7, 9]`. The two full blocks hold eight tokens, and block `9` holds two initialized entries. A service that supports partial-tail reuse can preserve all ten tokens and copy those two entries to a private tail before a divergent append, as in the preceding sharing example. A service that caches only complete blocks instead reuses eight tokens and prefills the remaining two. Both policies can be correct. One pays for tail handling; the other repeats a small amount of computation. Neither permits a new request to overwrite state that another owner still needs.

### Retention and eviction under pressure

A request finishing releases its active claim on KV state; it need not release the cache's claim. Dormant cached blocks remain occupied storage, retained in case another request reuses them. Conversely, a tool wait does not by itself create an obligation to retain those blocks. The service's retention policy decides whether the next turn finds state ready to use, must restore it, or must recompute it.

Reuse and reclamation must respect ownership. Before using a hit, the service acquires the references needed by the new request. Before recycling a block, it removes the cache's claim, confirms that no other owner needs the block, and waits for outstanding device operations that could access it to finish. A zero active-request count alone does not establish that the physical storage is safe to overwrite. Index updates and ownership changes must also prevent a lookup from acquiring a block while that block is being reclaimed.

A useful radix-cache policy is to retain complete paths from the root and evict unused leaves first. Removing a leaf preserves its shared ancestors for other requests; an ancestor becomes a candidate once no retained descendants require that path. Least-recently-used selection among eligible leaves is one concrete policy [@zheng2024sglang]. It expresses an expectation about future reuse, not a guarantee that the most valuable computation will survive. @Fig-vol3-radix-tree-cache shows the cascade: a dormant node with a cached child is not yet eligible, and evicting that child makes it a leaf that is.

::: {#fig-vol3-radix-tree-cache fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Leaf-First Eviction in a Radix Prefix Cache**: Each node stands for a run of tokens and the KV blocks that hold them, so a request's cached state is the path from the root to its node. Nodes on a running request's path stay active. Only dormant leaves are eligible, which is why the dormant Other-task node in panel (a) survives until its Final-turn child is evicted in panel (b). A least-recently-used policy would choose among the eligible leaves; it never removes an ancestor before its retained descendants." fig-alt="Two copies of a three-level tree. Panel a has an active shared-prefix root, an active repair-history node with an active test-log-turn leaf and a dormant rejected-branch leaf, and a dormant other-task node with a dormant final-turn leaf; the two dormant leaves are shaded as eligible for eviction. Panel b shows the final-turn leaf faded as evicted and the other-task node now shaded as an eligible dormant leaf. A legend defines active, dormant, eligible, and evicted."}
![](images/svg/radix_prefix_tree_architecture.svg)
:::

This prefix-closed residency rule simplifies serving; it is not a mathematical dependency of already stored tensors. Freeing a prefix block does not change the numerical values in a retained suffix block. However, the next full-attention step ordinarily needs the complete preceding KV state. A system that retains a suffix while discarding earlier blocks must reconstruct or restore the missing state before using that suffix as part of the complete history. Reconstruction requires the corresponding inputs and computation configuration to remain available.

Retention therefore trades occupied capacity against the work a future hit would avoid. Recency is useful evidence, but a recently created speculative branch may never run again, while an older shared prefix may serve many requests. Admission and eviction policies can consider expected reuse, reconstruction cost, and uniquely reclaimable storage. These considerations do not imply a universal priority formula. A policy must be evaluated against the workload and the capacity needed by active requests.

### Measuring reuse and exposing the contract

Potential token matches overstate the benefit when state is unavailable, sharing is disallowed, or the service rounds reuse down to a block boundary. Measure tokens actually served from reusable KV state. Over a specified set of requests, define the token-weighted prefix hit rate as

$$H_{\text{prefix}} = \frac{\sum_{i} S_{\text{match}}^{(i)}}{\sum_{i} S_{\text{prompt}}^{(i)}}$$ {#eq-hprefix}

Here $S_{\text{prompt}}^{(i)}$ is the number of prompt tokens in request $i$, and $S_{\text{match}}^{(i)}$ counts the prompt tokens whose compatible KV state the request actually reuses, after availability, permission, and boundary restrictions. The denominator includes all prompt tokens in the same request set and must be nonzero. In the full-block-only policy above, the reused count is eight, not the ten-token potential match. A service should distinguish reuse that requires restoration from reuse already resident on the accelerator.

```{python}
#| label: kv-prefix-hit-savings-calc
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ WHAT A PREFIX HIT AVOIDS
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-vol3-kvcache-radix-tree, "Measuring reuse" paragraph.
# │ Goal: Put a number on the prefill work a prefix hit avoids.
# │ Show: 1.34 GB of state; ~578 + ~22 trillion operations; ~169 ms at the
# │       sustained rate; ~5 ms weight-read floor for a short suffix pass.
# │ How: Registry model/node; linear 2NS plus causal attention 2LdS^2
# │      (@eq-appdx-prefill-long); sustained rate = node peak x MfuHigh x 0.9.
# │ Note: ChunkedIteration and PausedStateChoice reuse sustained_rate.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_int, fmt_memory, fmt_percent, MarkdownStr

class PrefixHit:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
    model = Models.Language.Llama3_70B
    node = Systems.Nodes.DGX_H100
    prefix_tokens = 4_096  # scenario: invariant instructions and tool schemas
    suffix_tokens = 32  # scenario: short novel suffix appended after a hit
    utilization = Literature.Training.MfuHigh * 0.9  # scenario: sustained prefill utilization

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    n_params = model.parameters.to("count").magnitude
    bytes_per_token = PhysicalBlockSizing.bytes_per_token
    state = prefix_tokens * bytes_per_token
    linear_ops = 2 * n_params * prefix_tokens * flop
    attention_ops = 2 * model.layers * model.hidden_dim * prefix_tokens**2 * flop
    sustained_rate = node.accelerators_per_node * node.accelerator.compute.peak_flops * utilization
    t_rebuild = ((linear_ops + attention_ops) / sustained_rate).to(ms)
    weights = model.size_in_bytes(BYTES_FP16)
    node_bw = node.accelerators_per_node * node.accelerator.memory.bandwidth
    t_weight_read = (weights / node_bw).to(ms)
    t_suffix_ops = (2 * n_params * suffix_tokens * flop / sustained_rate).to(ms)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(attention_ops < linear_ops, "Weight work must dominate at this prefix length")
    check(t_suffix_ops < t_weight_read, "A short suffix pass must sit below the ridge (weight-read bound)")
    check(150 < t_rebuild.magnitude < 190, "Prose describes roughly 170 ms of avoided prefill")
    check(t_weight_read < t_rebuild / 10, "The suffix floor must be far below the avoided prefill")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────────
    prefix_str = fmt_int(prefix_tokens)
    suffix_str = fmt_int(suffix_tokens)
    state_str = fmt_memory(state, unit=GB, precision=2)
    linear_str = fmt_int(linear_ops.to(flop).magnitude / 1e12)
    attention_str = fmt_int(attention_ops.to(flop).magnitude / 1e12)
    utilization_str = fmt_percent(utilization, precision=0, style="prose")
    rate_str = fmt_int(sustained_rate.to(TFLOPs / second).magnitude)
    rebuild_str = MarkdownStr(f"{fmt_int(t_rebuild.magnitude)} ms")
    weight_read_str = MarkdownStr(f"{fmt_int(t_weight_read.magnitude)} ms")
```

What a hit is worth follows from the same geometry. Suppose the repair agent's invariant instructions and tool schemas form a `{python} PrefixHit.prefix_str`-token prefix. Its KV state occupies `{python} PrefixHit.state_str` across the node. Reconstructing that state takes about `{python} PrefixHit.linear_str` trillion weight operations plus about `{python} PrefixHit.attention_str` trillion for causal attention (@eq-appdx-prefill-long). If the node sustains `{python} PrefixHit.utilization_str` of its peak 16-bit rate, about `{python} PrefixHit.rate_str` trillion operations per second, that is roughly `{python} PrefixHit.rebuild_str` of prefill on every turn that misses. A turn that hits and appends a `{python} PrefixHit.suffix_str`-token suffix still makes one pass over the weights, and a pass that short falls below the ridge, so one read of the weights bounds it at about `{python} PrefixHit.weight_read_str` (@eq-appdx-batched-step). Across a trajectory of many turns, the avoided prefill repeats at every turn whose prefix survives.

The hit rate in @eq-hprefix measures avoided reconstruction of prompt state, not a latency speedup or a billing discount. New suffix tokens still require prefill and attend to the preceding context; output tokens still require generation. Queueing, transfers, and the work left after a hit can dominate elapsed time. A falling hit rate warrants checking both sides of the interface: changes in serialization can shorten matches, while retention pressure, placement, or a configuration change can make matching state unavailable or incompatible.

For a hosted service, the caller needs an explicit reuse contract rather than assumptions about the hidden allocator. That contract should identify eligible inputs and configurations, sharing boundaries, supported cache hints or retention guarantees, and what the reported cached-token count means. Any documented expiration policy must be distinguished from a guarantee of residency. Expiration also couples the contract to tool waits. If a tool runs longer than the service's idle lifetime for cached state, the next turn finds no reusable prefix and pays the full prefill, which is the hosted form of the drop policy in @sec-vol3-kvcache-swapping. A harness that knows a wait will outlast that lifetime can plan for the miss rather than discover it in latency. Billing categories likewise need not expose where the tensors reside or how they are indexed. The caller controls its input layout and uses the controls actually offered; it cannot infer a particular tree, eviction policy, or physical placement from a discounted input-token count.

The application must remain correct on a cache miss: the selected context still supplies the model input, and the service computes the required state subject to the request's resource limits. Prefix caching reduces repeated work when compatible state is available. It does not remove the new work introduced by a large test log or retrieved observation. Scheduling that remaining prefill alongside ongoing generation is the next problem.

## Chunked Prefill Scheduling {#sec-vol3-kvcache-chunked-prefill}

Prefix reuse avoids processing an unchanged prefix, but a new observation still introduces work. When the repair agent submits selected integration-test output, the serving engine must process the uncached part of the serialized request before producing its response. Other requests may already be generating tokens on the same accelerators. If the engine runs the entire new prefill as one uninterrupted scheduling unit, those requests may have to wait for that unit to finish before their next decode step.

The conflict concerns when work runs, not which context the agent selected. Shortening the observation can reduce the work, but once the request reaches the server, the scheduler must share execution time among admitted requests. Chunked prefill divides the remaining prompt into smaller scheduling units so that the engine can advance ongoing decodes between, or alongside, those units [@agrawal2024sarathi]. It creates opportunities to serve other requests before the new prompt is complete.

### Preserving the causal computation

A prefill chunk is a span of tokens evaluated in a scheduling step. It is not a KV storage block. The scheduler chooses how much prompt work to run; the allocator maps the resulting attention state into physical blocks. Their sizes need not match.

For the causal attention used here, processing a later chunk requires the compatible per-layer KV state for the earlier prefix. Each query in the active chunk can attend to preceding tokens and to its own position, but not to later tokens in that chunk or in the remainder of the prompt. The engine preserves token positions and the causal mask while extending the stored state. It reads earlier keys and values rather than recomputing their projections from the beginning.

Thus chunking changes the execution schedule without changing the intended causal attention computation. That statement does not promise bitwise-identical floating-point results across different kernels or batching arrangements. Nor does avoiding repeated prefix projections make chunking free: later chunks still access earlier attention state, and smaller steps can add scheduling and kernel-launch overhead or use the hardware less efficiently.

### Choosing how much work to admit

A simple scheduler gives each iteration a token budget $C_{\text{budget}}$. With ordinary autoregressive decoding, each selected decode request contributes one new token position, and each selected prefill contributes the number of positions in its next chunk. An iteration that admits prefill chunks of $c_i$ tokens and a set $\mathcal{D}$ of decode requests must satisfy

$$\sum_{i} c_i + |\mathcal{D}| \le C_{\text{budget}}$$ {#eq-kv-token-budget}

and the admitted combination must also fit the available memory. A request whose prompt is only partly processed retains the completed prefix state while waiting for another turn.

Suppose the engine first reserves room for ongoing decode requests and then uses the remaining budget for prefill chunks. An existing request can make progress without waiting for another request's entire prompt. The new request, however, may need several iterations to complete its prefill, including waits while other work runs. Giving every iteration to existing decodes would protect them at the expense of new requests; admitting large prefills can reverse that priority. A useful policy must provide both decode responsiveness and eventual progress for prefills.

The budget bounds admitted token positions, not elapsed time. An iteration's duration also depends on the lengths of the contexts being attended to, the batch composition, kernel efficiency, memory traffic, and communication. Equal token counts therefore need not produce equal iteration times. A token budget alone cannot guarantee a particular gap between output tokens.

```{python}
#| label: kv-chunked-iteration-calc
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CHUNKED PREFILL: STALL VERSUS CHUNK
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-vol3-kvcache-chunked-prefill, paragraph after @eq-kv-token-budget.
# │ Goal: Show the scale of the decode-gap vs. prompt-completion trade.
# │ Show: ~5 ms decode-only step; ~162 ms monolithic prefill; ~22 ms per
# │       512-token chunked iteration; ~173 ms prompt completion; ~8x smaller gap.
# │ How: Weight-only step time max(Nb/beta, 2N tokens/pi) (@eq-appdx-batched-step)
# │      on the node with 16-bit weights; sustained rate from PrefixHit.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_int, fmt_multiple, MarkdownStr

class ChunkedIteration:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
    decodes = 32  # scenario: ongoing decode requests
    prompt_tokens = 4_096  # scenario: new uncached prefill
    chunk_tokens = 512  # scenario: prefill chunk per iteration
    n_params = PrefixHit.n_params
    rate = PrefixHit.sustained_rate
    t_weights = PrefixHit.t_weight_read

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    t_decode = max(t_weights, (2 * n_params * decodes * flop / rate).to(ms))
    t_mono = max(t_weights, (2 * n_params * prompt_tokens * flop / rate).to(ms))
    gap_mono = t_decode + t_mono
    n_chunks = prompt_tokens // chunk_tokens
    t_iter = max(t_weights, (2 * n_params * (chunk_tokens + decodes) * flop / rate).to(ms))
    t_chunked_done = n_chunks * t_iter
    gap_ratio = (gap_mono / t_iter).to("").magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(prompt_tokens % chunk_tokens == 0, "Chunks must tile the prompt")
    check(t_decode == t_weights, "Decode-only step must sit at the weight-read floor")
    check(t_iter > t_weights, "A 544-token iteration must be arithmetic-bound")
    check(t_mono < t_chunked_done < 1.1 * t_mono, "Chunking must delay prompt completion only modestly")
    check(6 < gap_ratio < 9, "Prose claims roughly an eightfold smaller worst gap")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────────
    decodes_str = fmt_int(decodes)
    prompt_str = fmt_int(prompt_tokens)
    chunk_str = fmt_int(chunk_tokens)
    iter_tokens_str = fmt_int(chunk_tokens + decodes)
    n_chunks_str = "eight" if n_chunks == 8 else fmt_int(n_chunks)
    t_decode_str = MarkdownStr(f"{fmt_int(t_decode.magnitude)} ms")
    t_mono_str = MarkdownStr(f"{fmt_int(t_mono.magnitude)} ms")
    gap_mono_str = MarkdownStr(f"{fmt_int(gap_mono.magnitude)} ms")
    t_iter_str = MarkdownStr(f"{fmt_int(t_iter.magnitude)} ms")
    t_done_str = MarkdownStr(f"{fmt_int(t_chunked_done.magnitude)} ms")
    gap_ratio_mult_str = fmt_multiple(round(gap_ratio))
```

A weight-only estimate still shows the scale of the trade. Apply @eq-appdx-batched-step to the eight-accelerator node with 16-bit weights, counting the token positions that @eq-kv-token-budget admits in one iteration and using the sustained rate assumed for the prefix-hit estimate. With `{python} ChunkedIteration.decodes_str` ongoing decodes and nothing else, each step sits at the weight-read floor of about `{python} ChunkedIteration.t_decode_str`. Admitting a `{python} ChunkedIteration.prompt_str`-token prefill as one unit adds about `{python} ChunkedIteration.t_mono_str` of arithmetic before those decodes run again, so their gap between tokens grows to about `{python} ChunkedIteration.gap_mono_str`. With `{python} ChunkedIteration.chunk_str`-token chunks, each iteration carries `{python} ChunkedIteration.iter_tokens_str` positions and takes about `{python} ChunkedIteration.t_iter_str`. The decodes now advance in each of the `{python} ChunkedIteration.n_chunks_str` iterations, so their worst gap is about `{python} ChunkedIteration.gap_ratio_mult_str` smaller, while the new prompt completes after about `{python} ChunkedIteration.t_done_str` instead of `{python} ChunkedIteration.t_mono_str`. Chunking buys existing streams a much shorter gap for a modest delay in the new request's first token. @Fig-vol3-chunked-timeline draws both schedules to scale. The estimate omits attention traffic, which grows with each chunk's context, and per-iteration overhead, so measured iterations run longer and the budget must come from measurement.

::: {#fig-vol3-chunked-timeline fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Monolithic vs. Chunked Prefill**: Both timelines use the weight-only estimate, on one time axis, for a `{python} ChunkedIteration.prompt_str`-token prefill arriving while `{python} ChunkedIteration.decodes_str` requests decode. Admitted as one unit (a), the prefill separates two decode tokens by about `{python} ChunkedIteration.gap_mono_str`. Split into `{python} ChunkedIteration.chunk_str`-token chunks (b), every iteration also advances the decodes, so the gap is one iteration of about `{python} ChunkedIteration.t_iter_str`, and the prompt finishes slightly later. Attention traffic and per-iteration overhead, omitted here, would lengthen every bar." fig-alt="Two horizontal timelines on a shared time axis with ticks at 0, 50, 100, and 150 milliseconds. Timeline a has one long prefill bar for 4,096 tokens followed by a short decode step, with output-token markers only at the start and the end and a bracket labeling the gap between decode tokens. Timeline b has eight equal bars labeled chunk 1 to chunk 8 plus decodes, with a token marker at every bar boundary and a bracket over the first bar. Each timeline marks where the prompt completes."}
![](images/svg/chunked_prefill_scheduling_timeline.svg)
:::

We can evaluate the trade-off by replaying the same arrival trace under different budgets. Measure time to first token for newly admitted requests, gaps between generated tokens for ongoing requests, completed useful work, and memory occupancy. Include queueing and scheduling waits in the latency measurements, and examine the slow requests rather than only the average. Client-visible streaming intervals may also include buffering and network delay, so they are not interchangeable with server iteration times.

Smaller chunks offer more frequent scheduling opportunities but may delay prompt completion and increase overhead. Larger chunks can improve execution efficiency while making other requests wait longer. The suitable budget is a workload-dependent operating choice, not a fixed consequence of the model's parameter count.

### Separating prefill and decode placement {#sec-vol3-kvcache-disaggregated}

Chunking shares execution time on a worker. Another option assigns prefill and decode to different workers, allowing their resources and parallelism to be selected separately [@zhong2024distserve]. This is a placement choice, not a prerequisite for chunked scheduling. A separated prefill worker can still process prompts in chunks.

Separation introduces a handoff. The decode worker needs compatible attention state, sufficient destination memory, and an agreed representation before it can continue the request. Transferring that state consumes bandwidth and may require layout conversion; requests can also queue at either worker. Even a transfer performed without host copies can contend for links and device memory bandwidth. Removing direct competition for compute does not remove these costs.

The operator therefore compares the latency and capacity of the complete path, including both queues and the handoff, rather than choosing separation from peak link bandwidth alone. For an agent using a hosted endpoint, these placement decisions usually remain inside the serving system. The agent observes their effects through request latency and service limits.

Chunking determines how an active request shares compute. It does not decide whether that request's attention state should remain on the accelerator while the agent waits for an external tool. Once generation pauses, retaining, moving, or reconstructing that state becomes a separate memory-management decision.

## Paused-State Policies {#sec-vol3-kvcache-swapping}

Return to the earlier integration-test wait, before its log arrives. The serving policy stipulated at the start of this chapter retains the repair's compatible attention state on the accelerator. Neither a completed model call nor a pending tool result requires that policy. Once the request no longer needs active computation, the serving operator can keep the state, move it elsewhere, or drop it and reconstruct it when needed. The choice trades accelerator capacity against storage, transfer, and computation at resumption. The model cannot make it. Memory is a resource bound, and invariant closure places resource bounds in the runtime below the model (principle \ref{pri-invariant-closure}), so the serving system owns the pause decision.

### What can actually be reclaimed

The relevant size is the physical allocation the policy can release, not the trajectory's logical context length alone. A paused trajectory may share prefix blocks with an active sibling. Removing the paused trajectory's reference does not free those blocks while the sibling still needs them. A block being read, written, or copied also remains unavailable for reuse until the operation completes. The allocation and sharing rules therefore precede any pause-policy calculation.

Moving state requires both space at the destination and a safe handoff. The runtime preserves the source until the copy completes successfully, records where the valid copy resides, and releases only blocks whose remaining ownership and in-flight operations permit reclamation. Before resumption, it must obtain accelerator capacity and make the required state accessible to the attention computation. During copying, source and destination storage can both be occupied. A host-memory budget must include this staging demand as well as already parked trajectories.

Dropping KV does not necessarily discard the information needed to continue the task. KV is derived from model inputs and configuration. Reconstruction requires those inputs to remain available, including the exact token sequence and applicable model, adapter, position, mask, and multimodal configuration. A summary of the conversation is not an exact substitute for that sequence. If a compatible prefix remains available, reconstruction can begin from it; otherwise the necessary prefix must be processed again. The policy must not assume that a hosted service exposes these controls to its caller.

### Comparing keep, move, and drop

The policies in @tbl-vol3-reclamation-policies differ in which resource carries the paused trajectory. None eliminates all the costs of resumption.

| **Policy** | **Accelerator capacity released**                 | **Work needed on return**                      | **Principal constraint**                          |
|:-----------|:--------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------|
| Keep       | None from the retained blocks                     | No restoration of those blocks                 | Retention competes with other allocations         |
| Move       | Reclaimable source blocks after a successful copy | Allocate and reload compatible state           | Destination capacity and contested transfer paths |
| Drop       | Reclaimable blocks after safe release             | Reconstruct missing state from retained inputs | Input availability and prefill capacity           |

: **Paused-state choices**: Restoration work is separate from queueing and processing the new observation, which can occur under every policy. {#tbl-vol3-reclamation-policies tbl-colwidths="[12,28,30,30]"}

Keeping state is reasonable when the pool has spare capacity and a likely return needs low restoration delay. Even a long pause does not make retention harmful if no competing work needs the blocks. Under pressure, moving state can free accelerator capacity while avoiding repeated prefill. Dropping it can be preferable when a return is unlikely, host capacity is scarce, or reconstruction is less costly than preserving and transferring the state. The operator also has to respect the isolation rules that govern who may access a saved prefix.

Storage beyond host memory is another possible destination, not a mandatory stage for human approval or any other kind of wait. Its usefulness depends on available capacity, transfer and retrieval costs, compatibility at the eventual return, and the probability that the state will be reused. A serialized KV copy is not by itself a durable record of the task's inputs, actions, and evidence.

### A bounded comparison during the test wait

```{python}
#| label: kv-paused-state-choice-calc
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ PAUSED-STATE CHOICE: RELOAD VERSUS RECOMPUTE DURING A TOOL WAIT
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-vol3-kvcache-swapping, the bounded test-wait comparison,
# │          @eq-kv-reload-ratio, and @fig-vol3-swapping-tradeoff.
# │ Goal: Separate capacity occupancy, transfer work, and restoration delay,
# │       with stage durations derived from registry rates.
# │ Show: 10.74 GB; 21 ms each way, 42 ms round trip; ~1.3 s recompute; ~62x,
# │       ~15x at a quarter of link bandwidth; 483.18 GB·s held;
# │       44.98 s on-demand and 44.96 s prefetch release windows.
# │ How: Registry KV geometry; per-accelerator host link x 8 (tensor-parallel
# │      shards move in parallel, a scenario assumption); sustained prefill
# │      rate shared with PrefixHit; attention term omitted (weight work only).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_int, fmt_memory, fmt_qty, fmt_time, fmt_bandwidth, fmt_multiple, MarkdownStr

class PausedStateChoice:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ───────────────────────────────────────────────────
    model = Models.Language.Llama3_70B
    node = Systems.Nodes.DGX_H100
    context_tokens = 32_768  # scenario: fully initialized state, no sharing
    block_tokens = 16  # scenario allocation granularity, not a recommendation
    runtime_reserve = 20 * GB  # scenario, same aggregate-node baseline
    wait = 45 * second  # stipulated integration-test wait
    n_acc = node.accelerators_per_node
    link_per_acc = node.accelerator.interconnect.bandwidth  # registry host link, per direction
    rate = PrefixHit.sustained_rate  # scenario sustained prefill rate
    quarter = 0.25  # scenario: links sustain a quarter of rated bandwidth

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    blocks = (context_tokens + block_tokens - 1) // block_tokens
    state = calc_kv_cache_size(
        model.layers,
        model.kv_heads,
        model.hidden_dim // model.heads,
        blocks * block_tokens,
        1,
        BYTES_FP16,
    )
    bytes_per_token = state / (blocks * block_tokens)
    pool = n_acc * node.accelerator.memory.capacity - model.size_in_bytes(BYTES_FP16) - runtime_reserve
    n_params = model.parameters.to("count").magnitude
    link = n_acc * link_per_acc
    copy_out = (state / link).to(ms)
    copy_in = (state / link).to(ms)
    reconstruct = (2 * n_params * context_tokens * flop / rate).to(second)
    ratio = (reconstruct / copy_in).to("").magnitude
    ratio_quarter = ratio * quarter
    reload_over_recompute = (bytes_per_token * rate / (2 * n_params * flop * link)).to("").magnitude
    held_occupancy = state * wait
    transfer_work = copy_out + copy_in
    released_on_demand = wait - copy_out
    released_prefetch = wait - copy_out - copy_in

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(context_tokens % block_tokens == 0, "No partial-tail waste in this example")
    check(state.to(byte).magnitude == 10_737_418_240, "Registry geometry must give the stated payload")
    check(0 < state < pool, "One state must fit the aggregate pool; shard fit is separate")
    check(abs(reload_over_recompute * ratio - 1) < 1e-9, "Context length must cancel in the reload/recompute ratio")
    check(55 < ratio < 70, "Prose claims reload is about sixty times faster")
    check(ratio_quarter > 10, "Prose claims reload still wins by over ten times at a quarter of link bandwidth")
    check(transfer_work < wait / 1000, "The round trip must be under a tenth of a percent of the wait")
    check(abs(held_occupancy.to(GB * second).magnitude - 483.1838208) < 1e-6, "Occupancy is capacity times time, not a monetary cost")
    check(released_prefetch < released_on_demand < wait, "Prefetch reserves the destination earlier than on-demand reload")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ────────────────────────────────────────────────
    context_str = fmt_int(context_tokens)
    block_str = fmt_int(block_tokens)
    state_str = fmt_memory(state, unit=GB, precision=2)
    wait_str = fmt_time(wait, "second", precision=0)
    link_per_acc_str = fmt_bandwidth(link_per_acc, unit=GB / second, precision=0)
    link_str = fmt_bandwidth(link, unit=GB / second, precision=0)
    out_str = MarkdownStr(f"{fmt_int(copy_out.magnitude)} ms")
    in_str = MarkdownStr(f"{fmt_int(copy_in.magnitude)} ms")
    transfer_str = MarkdownStr(f"{fmt_int(transfer_work.magnitude)} ms")
    reconstruct_str = fmt_time(reconstruct, "second", precision=1)
    ratio_mult_str = fmt_multiple(round(ratio))
    ratio_quarter_mult_str = fmt_multiple(round(ratio_quarter))
    held_str = fmt_qty(held_occupancy, unit=GB * second, precision=2)
    demand_free_str = fmt_time(released_on_demand, "second", precision=2)
    prefetch_free_str = fmt_time(released_prefetch, "second", precision=2)
```

Consider the chapter's `{python} PausedStateChoice.context_str`-token state during the `{python} PausedStateChoice.wait_str` integration-test wait on the same sharded node. For this comparison, all historical KV entries have been computed, the `{python} PausedStateChoice.block_str`-token blocks are full, and none is shared or in flight. The uniquely reclaimable payload is therefore `{python} PausedStateChoice.state_str`. Metadata and transfer buffers are excluded from this payload; the runtime must budget them separately.

The stage durations follow from registry rates. Each accelerator holds one-eighth of the tensor-parallel state and reaches host memory over its own `{python} PausedStateChoice.link_per_acc_str` link, so if the eight transfers proceed in parallel the node moves state at up to $\beta_{\text{link}} =$ `{python} PausedStateChoice.link_str`. Moving the complete state out then takes about `{python} PausedStateChoice.out_str`, and restoring it takes the same. Reconstruction instead repeats the prefill.
