At the sustained rate assumed for the prefix-hit estimate, its $2NS$ weight operations take about `{python} PausedStateChoice.reconstruct_str`; the attention term of @eq-appdx-prefill-long, omitted here, would only lengthen it. These are sustained-rate estimates for an uncontended node, and an operator replaces them with stage durations measured under the intended load. All policies still need to process the new test observation, so that common work is outside the comparison.

Both estimates grow linearly with the retained length $S$, so their ratio does not depend on it:

$$\frac{T_{\text{reload}}}{T_{\text{recompute}}} = \frac{S \, m_{\text{token}} / \beta_{\text{link}}}{2 N S / \pi} = \frac{m_{\text{token}} \, \pi}{2 N \, \beta_{\text{link}}}$$ {#eq-kv-reload-ratio}

Here $N$ is the parameter count and $\pi$ the sustained prefill rate. @Eq-kv-reload-ratio is the restricted comparison of @sec-vol3-appendix-inference-queueing applied to the reference node. Reload is about `{python} PausedStateChoice.ratio_mult_str` faster than reconstruction, and still about `{python} PausedStateChoice.ratio_quarter_mult_str` faster if the links sustain only a quarter of their rated bandwidth. On this node, reconstruction is the better way back only when host memory or the link, not accelerator time, is the scarce resource.

Keeping the state occupies `{python} PausedStateChoice.state_str` $\times$ `{python} PausedStateChoice.wait_str` $\approx$ `{python} PausedStateChoice.held_str` during the wait, with the calculation using the unrounded payload. This memory-time product measures capacity occupancy. It is not a dollar charge or evidence that useful work was displaced.

Moving it out immediately, then reloading only when the test returns, makes the blocks available after the outward copy completes. They can serve other work for `{python} PausedStateChoice.wait_str` $-$ `{python} PausedStateChoice.out_str` $=$ `{python} PausedStateChoice.demand_free_str` before the return. The policy performs `{python} PausedStateChoice.transfer_str` of transfer work in total, but only the inward stage lies after the return, adding `{python} PausedStateChoice.in_str` of restoration delay under these estimates. Dropping the state avoids that transfer work but requires about `{python} PausedStateChoice.reconstruct_str` of reconstruction when it is needed again. Safe release is assumed to have negligible duration in this example; a real measurement must include any outstanding operations.

If the return time were known exactly, prefetch could finish the inward copy just as the test ends. Reserving the full destination allocation at the start of that copy leaves a release window of `{python} PausedStateChoice.wait_str` $-$ `{python} PausedStateChoice.out_str` $-$ `{python} PausedStateChoice.in_str` $=$ `{python} PausedStateChoice.prefetch_free_str`. This hides restoration delay from this particular return; it does not remove the transfers or their destination allocation. It is a conditional schedule, not a guarantee supplied by a long average wait.

The same comparison applies at every context length and wait. @Fig-vol3-swapping-tradeoff places the test wait among the regimes that the reload round trip and host capacity define when accelerator memory has a competing use. Under that pressure, keeping state pays only for waits shorter than the round trip, which grows linearly with context and is `{python} PausedStateChoice.transfer_str` here. Longer waits favor moving the state, which frees accelerator memory for nearly the whole wait at a resume cost of one reload. Waits measured in minutes, such as human approvals, make the decision turn on host capacity, colder storage, or reconstruction.

::: {#fig-vol3-swapping-tradeoff fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Keep, Offload, or Park a Paused Trajectory**: Decision regimes over expected tool wait and context length, both on log scales, for a paused trajectory whose accelerator memory has a competing use. The diagonal is the reload round trip, twice the state size divided by host-link bandwidth, so it grows linearly with context; waits to its left end before the state could move out and back. The dashed boundary reflects host-memory pressure rather than a fixed duration, and the marked point is the 32,768-token, 45-second integration test." fig-alt="Log-log chart with expected tool wait from 1 ms to 1 hour on the horizontal axis and context length from 2,048 to 131,072 tokens on the vertical axis. A diagonal line separates a retain region on the left from an offload-to-host-memory region; a dashed vertical line near 1 minute separates a park-or-drop region on the right. A marked point at 32,768 tokens and about 45 seconds is labeled as the worked example."}
![](images/svg/break_even_swapping_tradeoff.svg)
:::

### Uncertain returns and competing transfers

A test can finish earlier than predicted, fail quickly, or run longer. Early completion exposes unfinished restoration. An early prefetch followed by a late return occupies accelerator memory again while no generation occurs. If the trajectory never resumes, the inward copy was unnecessary. A policy therefore needs a forecast of return behavior and an acceptable restoration delay, not just a comparison between the average wait and an isolated copy time.

Transfers also compete. Several paused trajectories may return together, sharing a host-memory channel, device link, or storage path. Summing nominal device-link rates is justified only if the data layout and independent paths actually sustain that aggregate rate.

```{python}
#| label: kv-return-burst-calc
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CORRELATED-RETURN BURST
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-vol3-kvcache-swapping, "Uncertain returns and competing transfers".
# │ Goal: Size the reload burst when many paused trajectories return together.
# │ Show: 32 returns; 344 GB; >= 0.67 s at the full aggregate link rate;
# │       the last reload waits ~32x the isolated reload.
# │ How: PausedStateChoice state and aggregate link rate (an upper bound on the
# │      shared path; registry host-memory bandwidth is higher, so links bind).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_int, fmt_time, fmt_multiple, MarkdownStr

class ReturnBurst:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
    returns = 32  # scenario: paused repairs whose tests finish together
    state = PausedStateChoice.state
    link = PausedStateChoice.link
    host_bw = PausedStateChoice.node.host_memory_bw

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    burst = returns * state
    t_burst = (burst / link).to(second)
    slowdown = (t_burst / PausedStateChoice.copy_in).to("").magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(link < host_bw, "The host links, not host memory bandwidth, must bind at the aggregate rate")
    check(burst < PausedStateChoice.pool, "The returning states must fit the accelerator pool")
    check(abs(slowdown - returns) < 1e-9, "Serialized reloads scale with the number of returns")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────────
    returns_str = fmt_int(returns)
    burst_str = MarkdownStr(f"{fmt_int(burst.to(GB).magnitude)} GB")
    t_burst_str = fmt_time(t_burst, "second", precision=2)
    slowdown_mult_str = fmt_multiple(round(slowdown))
```

Suppose `{python} ReturnBurst.returns_str` paused repairs on the node return within the same moment. Their states total about `{python} ReturnBurst.burst_str`, which take at least `{python} ReturnBurst.t_burst_str` to reload even at the full aggregate rate of the eight host links. The last reload in the queue therefore waits about `{python} ReturnBurst.slowdown_mult_str` as long as the isolated `{python} PausedStateChoice.in_str` reload, and any narrower shared path lengthens the burst. The operator must account for the contested path, its queue, and the accelerator capacity needed to receive the returning states. Restoration measurements without competing traffic do not establish the delay under a burst.

Some transfer can overlap other work, but dependencies determine which work. In the full-attention baseline, processing new observation tokens needs access to the relevant historical keys and values. A schedule cannot simply declare all historical reload hidden behind processing that depends on it. Earlier prefetch or a supported layer- or block-wise pipeline can expose overlap; each still needs a valid dependency order and enough memory for the in-flight data.

### Reclamation versus approximation {#sec-vol3-kvcache-intrasequence}

Keep, move, and reconstruct compare ways to make the required state available without intentionally deleting selected historical attention entries from the chosen full-attention computation. A different policy may prune entries, use a restricted attention window, or reduce KV precision. Those choices change the computation or its numerical representation and require their own task-quality and implementation validation. They are not universally invalid, but low attention weight on earlier queries does not establish irrelevance to a future query.

Attention sinks show why the simplest approximation fails. Softmax weights at each query sum to one, so later queries deposit attention mass they cannot place elsewhere on the first few positions of the sequence. A sliding window that evicts those initial tokens removes that stabilizing mass and degrades generation once the sequence outgrows the window; retaining a handful of initial tokens beside the recent window restores stable generation over long streams [@xiao2024streamingllm]. Score-based policies go further and keep the entries that have accumulated the most attention [@zhang2023h2o] or that showed importance soon after they were written [@liu2023scissorhands]. Both families assume that past attention predicts future need.

Agent trajectories break that assumption in three recurring ways. A constraint stated early, such as the repair's API restriction or a read-only credential, can draw little attention through many intervening tool turns and then decide the final edit. An identifier such as a commit hash, process ID, or transaction token can stay dormant for many turns until a command must quote it exactly. Tool-schema delimiters in the prefix govern the structure of every later call, yet any single step may attend to them weakly; losing them produces malformed calls rather than a slightly worse answer. An approximation must be evaluated on such dependencies, rather than accepted solely because it reduces stored bytes. Conversely, preserving KV does not guarantee a correct repair, bitwise-identical execution, or valid external actions. It preserves derived computation under its compatibility conditions; task verification remains separate.

The pause policy determines how long reclaimable blocks remain occupied and what demand returns later. Capacity planning must now combine those lifetimes with the physical allocations of all the trajectories sharing the node.

## Capacity for Agent Workloads {#sec-vol3-kvcache-capacity-planning}

A paused repair can occupy attention-state storage without generating tokens, while a new repair needs both storage and execution time. Keeping, moving, or dropping paused state therefore changes how many trajectories the serving system can hold, but does not by itself determine how quickly it completes work. Capacity planning must separate a physical fit calculation from a service-rate claim.

The distinction also changes what counts as demand. Logical contexts may overlap through shared blocks, generated continuations need private allocation, and dormant prefixes may be discarded without interrupting an active request. Summing every trajectory's logical KV footprint would charge shared storage repeatedly; counting only currently decoding requests would omit other state that still occupies the pool. The useful starting point is the set of unique physical blocks that the chosen policy must retain.

### A resident-fit bound {#sec-vol3-kv-capacity-formulations}

Consider equal-length requests with prompt length $S$ and an output allowance $K_{\max}$. The allocation estimate rounds each private region up to a whole block. Without sharing, each request pays for its entire prompt and output allowance. With an available compatible common prefix, the pool pays for that prefix once and for each request's remaining prompt and private output separately. The common prefix must end on a block boundary for this simple decomposition; a partial shared tail requires the copy-on-write accounting taught earlier.

The pool is what remains of accelerator memory after the weights and runtime reserve,

$$M_{\text{pool}} = M_{\text{HBM}} - M_{\text{weights}} - M_{\text{runtime}}$$ {#eq-mkv-pool}

and a planner withholds a further headroom fraction $\theta$ of it. With blocks of $p$ tokens, a block-aligned common prefix of $S_{\text{common}}$ tokens, and $B$ resident requests, the blocks demanded must fit the usable blocks:

$$\left\lceil \frac{S_{\text{common}}}{p} \right\rceil + B \left\lceil \frac{S + K_{\max} - S_{\text{common}}}{p} \right\rceil \le \left\lfloor \frac{(1-\theta)\, M_{\text{pool}}}{p \, m_{\text{token}}} \right\rfloor$$ {#eq-kv-demand-shared}

The resident-fit bound is the largest $B$ that satisfies @eq-kv-demand-shared. Setting $S_{\text{common}} = 0$ recovers the unshared case, in which every request pays for its whole prompt. The common term is paid once, so sharing helps most when the common prefix is a large fraction of each prompt and the private region, including the output allowance, is small.

The estimate in notebook \ref{nbk-05-sizing-hbm-for-multi-turn-agent} applies those rules to the same node and model used for the footprint calculation. It reserves a complete output allowance rather than predicting an average final length. The additional headroom is a hypothetical planning choice, not an empirically established safety threshold.

```{python}
#| label: compute-agent-capacity
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: nbk-05-sizing-hbm-for-multi-turn-agent and resident-time prose.
# │ Goal: Bound resident requests with unique, block-rounded KV allocation.
# │ Show: 41 unshared or 138 shared snapshots; memory-only residence constraints.
# │ How: Registry model/node, explicit reserve/headroom, and whole-block counts.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from math import ceil, floor
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.physics.agents import calc_kv_cache_bytes_per_token
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_int, fmt_memory, fmt_percent, fmt_time, fmt_magnitude

class AgentCapacity:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ───────────────────────────────────────────────────
    _model = Models.Language.Llama3_70B
    _node = Systems.Nodes.DGX_H100
    runtime_reserve = 20 * GB  # scenario: aggregate activation/runtime reserve
    headroom = 0.10  # hypothetical extra fraction withheld from the KV pool
    context = 32_768  # scenario: serialized input tokens per request
    output = 2_048  # scenario: maximum private output tokens
    common = 24_576  # scenario: identical, compatible, shareable prefix tokens
    block_tokens = 16  # scenario: allocation granularity, not a recommendation
    generation = 5 * second  # hypothetical residence component, not a benchmark
    wait = 45 * second  # hypothetical tool wait with retained state

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    bytes_per_token = calc_kv_cache_bytes_per_token(_model, bytes_per_elem=BYTES_FP16)
    node_hbm = _node.accelerators_per_node * _node.accelerator.memory.capacity
    weights = _model.size_in_bytes(BYTES_FP16)
    pool = node_hbm - weights - runtime_reserve
    block_bytes = block_tokens * bytes_per_token
    usable_blocks = floor(((1 - headroom) * pool / block_bytes).to("").magnitude)
    usable = usable_blocks * block_bytes
    unshared_blocks = ceil((context + output) / block_tokens)
    common_blocks = ceil(common / block_tokens)
    private_blocks = ceil((context + output - common) / block_tokens)
    unshared_bytes = unshared_blocks * block_bytes
    common_bytes = common_blocks * block_bytes
    private_bytes = private_blocks * block_bytes
    fit_unshared = usable_blocks // unshared_blocks
    fit_shared = (usable_blocks - common_blocks) // private_blocks
    retained_time = generation + wait
    retained_rate = fit_unshared / retained_time
    released_rate = fit_unshared / generation

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(pool.to(GB).magnitude > 0, "Weights and reserve must leave a positive KV pool")
    check(0 <= common <= context and common % block_tokens == 0, "Shared prefix must be valid and block-aligned")
    check(usable <= (1 - headroom) * pool, "Block rounding must not exceed the usable pool")
    check(unshared_blocks == common_blocks + private_blocks, "Aligned shared/private blocks must recover the unshared count")
    check(fit_unshared == 41 and fit_shared == 138, "Canonical resident-fit bounds must remain 41/138")
    check(fit_unshared * unshared_blocks <= usable_blocks < (fit_unshared + 1) * unshared_blocks, "Unshared fit must be maximal")
    check(
        common_blocks + fit_shared * private_blocks <= usable_blocks < common_blocks + (fit_shared + 1) * private_blocks, "Shared fit must be maximal"
    )
    check(retained_rate < released_rate, "Removing positive waiting residence must loosen this memory-only constraint")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ────────────────────────────────────────────────
    precision_bits_str = fmt_int(BYTES_FP16.to(bit).magnitude)
    reserve_str = fmt_memory(runtime_reserve, unit=GB, precision=0)
    pool_str = fmt_memory(pool, unit=GB, precision=1)
    headroom_str = fmt_percent(headroom, precision=0, style="prose")
    context_str = fmt_int(context)
    output_str = fmt_int(output)
    common_str = fmt_int(common)
    block_tokens_str = fmt_int(block_tokens)
    block_bytes_str = fmt_memory(block_bytes, unit=MB, precision=3)
    usable_blocks_str = fmt_int(usable_blocks)
    unshared_blocks_str = fmt_int(unshared_blocks)
    common_blocks_str = fmt_int(common_blocks)
    private_blocks_str = fmt_int(private_blocks)
    unshared_bytes_str = fmt_memory(unshared_bytes, unit=GB, precision=2)
    common_bytes_str = fmt_memory(common_bytes, unit=GB, precision=2)
    private_bytes_str = fmt_memory(private_bytes, unit=GB, precision=2)
    fit_unshared_str = fmt_int(fit_unshared)
    fit_shared_str = fmt_int(fit_shared)
    generation_str = fmt_time(generation, unit=second, precision=0)
    wait_str = fmt_time(wait, unit=second, precision=0)
    retained_time_str = fmt_time(retained_time, unit=second, precision=0)
    retained_rate_value_str = fmt_magnitude(retained_rate, unit=1 / second, precision=2)
    released_rate_value_str = fmt_magnitude(released_rate, unit=1 / second, precision=1)
```

::: {#nbk-05-sizing-hbm-for-multi-turn-agent .callout-notebook title="From logical contexts to physical fit"}

**Problem**: How many complete request snapshots fit when a common prefix is stored once rather than copied for every request?

**Variables**: The Llama-3 70B model uses `{python} AgentCapacity.precision_bits_str`-bit weights and KV state on the DGX H100 node. After weights and the stipulated `{python} AgentCapacity.reserve_str` runtime reserve, its KV pool (@eq-mkv-pool) is `{python} AgentCapacity.pool_str`. Withhold an additional `{python} AgentCapacity.headroom_str`. Each request has `{python} AgentCapacity.context_str` input tokens and an allowance of `{python} AgentCapacity.output_str` output tokens; `{python} AgentCapacity.common_str` input tokens form the common prefix. Blocks hold `{python} AgentCapacity.block_tokens_str` tokens, or `{python} AgentCapacity.block_bytes_str` of KV state across the node.

**Math**: Divide the remaining pool by bytes per block and round down, giving `{python} AgentCapacity.usable_blocks_str` usable blocks. An unshared request occupies `{python} AgentCapacity.unshared_blocks_str` blocks (`{python} AgentCapacity.unshared_bytes_str`). Dividing the usable block count by that request count and rounding down gives `{python} AgentCapacity.fit_unshared_str` resident requests. With sharing, subtract the common prefix's `{python} AgentCapacity.common_blocks_str` blocks (`{python} AgentCapacity.common_bytes_str`) once, then divide by `{python} AgentCapacity.private_blocks_str` private blocks per request (`{python} AgentCapacity.private_bytes_str`). Rounding down gives `{python} AgentCapacity.fit_shared_str` resident requests.

**Systems insight**: Sharing changes the physical storage bound without reducing every request's logical context or eliminating its decoding work. These counts assume balanced sharding and adequate per-device runtime space. They are resident-fit bounds for the stated allocation, not safe admission limits or measured service rates.

:::

Real requests have different lengths and overlap patterns. An admission policy must account for the blocks it promises to active requests, upcoming output growth, and temporary allocations during transfers or copies. A mean footprint cannot guarantee that the next set of requests fits. The node-wide bound also needs a per-device check because a free block on one device does not compensate for an exhausted shard on another.

### Residence time and service rate {#sec-vol3-kv-workload-dynamics}

A fit bound describes simultaneous occupancy. Turning it into a rate requires a time model with the same accounting boundary. For a stable flow of requests through resident storage, Little's law [@little1961] states that the mean resident request count $\bar{N}$ equals the arrival rate $\lambda$ multiplied by the mean time $\bar{W}$ each request occupies that storage, $\bar{N} = \lambda \bar{W}$; rearranged as $\lambda = \bar{N} / \bar{W}$, it turns a slot count into a rate. Here each counted request is one generation-and-tool-wait cycle, not an entire repair task. In a stationary regime without accumulating unfinished work, arrivals and completed cycles have the same long-run rate.

For a deliberately simplified calculation, reserve an equal unshared slot for each admitted cycle throughout its resident interval, using the preceding notebook's `{python} AgentCapacity.fit_unshared_str`-slot bound. Stipulate `{python} AgentCapacity.generation_str` of generation residence and `{python} AgentCapacity.wait_str` of tool waiting. Retaining every slot through both phases gives `{python} AgentCapacity.retained_time_str` of residence. Dividing the slot count by that residence time yields a memory-only upper constraint of `{python} AgentCapacity.retained_rate_value_str` turns/s. If the entire slot can instead be released for the wait, dividing by generation residence alone loosens the constraint to `{python} AgentCapacity.released_rate_value_str` turns/s.

The second calculation omits prefill, restoration residence, transfer contention, queueing, and allocation overlap. It also assumes that every slot is independently reclaimable; shared blocks still used by another request cannot be released with one waiting trajectory. The calculation is therefore neither a throughput prediction nor evidence of a service speedup. Compute or transfer capacity can bind before memory residence does, and a policy that saves byte-seconds can still miss a resume deadline.

Even a correct mean relation does not bound bursts. Several tools can return together, or one turn can spawn multiple candidates, creating demand that a time average conceals. Planning must test the intended distribution of prompt lengths, output growth, branching, and waits against both physical availability and latency targets. The average is an accounting check; the workload and scheduler determine whether a particular admission policy is adequate.

### Telemetry that explains pressure {#sec-vol3-kv-telemetry-metrics}

Allocated occupancy alone cannot distinguish useful caching from impending allocation failure. A nearly full pool of discardable dormant prefixes may accept a new request after cheap reclamation. The same occupancy with all blocks pinned by active work leaves little room for growth. @Tbl-vol3-kv-pool-states separates the physical states needed to interpret that difference.

| **Pool state**            | **Accounting and consequence**                                                                                                                                              |
|:--------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Active or pinned          | Count each physical block once, even when several requests reference it. It cannot be reclaimed while any required owner or operation still uses it.                        |
| Reserved or in flight     | Count additional blocks unavailable for admission because they are reserved or being populated, copied, or transferred. Exclude blocks already counted as active or pinned. |
| Reclaimable dormant cache | Count retained blocks that have no required active or in-flight use and can be discarded under the service's policy. Reclaiming them can remove a future reuse opportunity. |
| Genuinely free            | Count blocks immediately available to allocate, with no live owner, unfinished operation, or reservation.                                                                   |

: **Physical pool accounting**: Apply the rows in order so each block belongs to exactly one category at a given instant. Logical references are tracked separately from physical storage. {#tbl-vol3-kv-pool-states tbl-colwidths="[28,72]"}

A block being copied while an active request still references it belongs in the first row; its newly allocated destination belongs in the second until ready. A dormant prefix is reclaimable only when its ownership and in-flight-use conditions permit release. This partition makes remaining allocation options visible without counting shared blocks repeatedly or assuming that an eviction request frees memory immediately.

The storage view needs measurements of work and delay alongside it. Record offered requests and prompt/output token volumes, actual reused prompt tokens under the denominator defined earlier, eviction and restoration traffic, recomputed tokens, and the distribution of waits and resumes. Compare admission delay, time to first token, inter-token latency, and resume latency with explicit targets under the same workload. A high reuse fraction can coexist with long queues, while an eviction can be harmless if the removed prefix would never have been used again.

Repeated eviction followed by reload or recomputation is evidence of churn. If that churn accompanies worsening tail latency or falling completed work at comparable offered load, it motivates a change in admission, retention, or scheduling. No fixed occupied fraction establishes that diagnosis across allocators and workloads. An application caller with only provider-exposed metrics should make claims within that visibility boundary; detailed physical-pool diagnosis belongs to the serving operator.

The storage bound and telemetry now support a complete local decision. A serving operator can identify which state must remain, which bytes can be reclaimed, and what work or delay reclamation introduces. The following self-check combines those judgments before the chapter closes.

::: {#chk-vol3-kv-capacity-diagnosis .callout-checkpoint title="Fit, pressure, and completed work"}

Two runs report the same occupied fraction, but one holds mostly dormant prefixes and the other holds mostly active state.

- [ ] **Physical ownership**: Can you explain why their immediate admission options differ and how a shared block should be counted?
- [ ] **Resident-fit bound**: In the notebook, how would removing all common-prefix sharing change the bound, and why would neither count establish throughput?
- [ ] **Residence estimate**: If the hypothetical wait doubles while generation residence stays fixed, how does the retained-slot rate constraint change?
- [ ] **Policy evidence**: Which workload, restoration, and latency measurements would distinguish useful eviction from repeated churn?

:::

## Fallacies and Pitfalls {#sec-vol3-kv-cache-fallacies}

The common errors promote a storage fact into a stronger claim about information, correctness, or performance. Keeping those boundaries separate prevents an optimization from silently changing the problem it was meant to solve.

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Fallacy**: *A resident-fit count is a throughput guarantee.*

The sizing notebook counts physical blocks under a stated sharing pattern and output allowance. It does not count how quickly the device processes those tokens or how long admitted requests wait for service. The residence calculation adds one necessary time constraint under deliberately restricted assumptions, not a sufficient performance model. Validate an admission policy against offered load, growth and burst behavior, and the latency targets that define useful service.
:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Pitfall**: *Always moving paused state out of accelerator memory.*

A long pause makes retained storage expensive only when that storage has a competing use. A quiet pool may benefit from keeping state ready, whereas a busy pool may justify movement or recomputation. Shared and in-flight blocks also limit the memory actually released. Compare uniquely reclaimable storage with transfer work, reconstruction cost, expected reuse, and the resume deadline rather than treating a tool boundary as a mandatory eviction event.
:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Fallacy**: *Compatible cached attention state proves that its evidence is current.*

State computed from the repair's r17 tokens can remain numerically compatible with those same tokens after the workspace changes to r18. That compatibility says nothing about whether the r17 failure supports a claim about r18. Refreshing the logical request with the r18 observation changes the relevant prefix, while the old failure can remain valid historical evidence. Numerical reuse and source applicability require separate checks.
:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Pitfall**: *Treating KV storage as the authoritative task record.*

Attention tensors encode reusable computation for a particular input and model configuration; retaining or serializing them does not replace a record of the source versions, observations, and acceptance evidence the task needs. Conversely, discarding them need not discard that information when reconstruction inputs remain available. Recomputing under a compatible execution can restore usable attention state, but bitwise equality across implementations and precision choices is a separate numerical requirement.
:::

## Summary {#sec-vol3-kv-cache-summary}

The repair's selected context becomes a physical allocation only through the serving system's policy. Attention geometry determines the storage per token; blocks determine allocation granularity and sharing; prefix compatibility and availability determine which computation can be reused. Scheduling and paused-state policy then decide when that storage is occupied and what other work must wait. None of these mechanisms decides whether the repair's evidence applies to the current source version.

::: {.callout-takeaways title="Managing derived attention state"}

* **Token state has a physical footprint**: For the chosen full-attention architecture and precision, retained length determines KV storage. A context that fits the model's interface can still exceed the deployment's available pool, and a node-wide estimate must respect per-device placement and runtime space.
* **Physical blocks, not references, consume capacity**: Allocation rounds private state to blocks, while compatible shared state is stored once. Reclaiming a trajectory frees only blocks no remaining owner or unfinished operation requires; logical context size is not automatically reclaimable memory.
* **Reuse needs compatibility and availability**: Matching input permits reuse only when the appropriate state remains accessible under the service's sharing rules. A cache hit establishes neither source freshness nor task acceptance, so preserving a hit must not prevent a necessary context refresh.
* **Retention and scheduling spend different resources**: Chunking work can protect ongoing decodes while delaying prompt completion. Keeping, moving, or reconstructing paused state exchanges memory residence for work and resume delay; the appropriate choice depends on competing demand and service constraints.
* **Fit bounds need workload evidence**: A storage calculation establishes what can reside under explicit assumptions. Sustainable service also depends on execution, transfer, and queueing. Interpret occupancy through ownership and reclaimability, then test reuse and eviction policies against completed work and latency targets.

:::

Attention state derived from the token prefix (principle \ref{pri-vol3-prefix-coherence}) creates an opportunity to reuse work, not an obligation to keep every computed tensor resident. Block ownership and residence accounting price that opportunity. Authority still stays with the source (principle \ref{pri-vol3-source-authority}); a cheaper continuation does not make an old observation evidence about a changed artifact.

::: {.callout-chapter-connection title="From reusable computation to durable information"}

The repair may need its source-version history, unresolved checks, and acceptance evidence after the serving session ends. KV state can itself be moved or serialized, so storage location alone does not define this boundary. The unresolved problem is which information should persist, how it is identified and updated, and how a later request obtains evidence appropriate to its task. @Sec-vol3-long-term-memory develops that durable-information contract.

:::
